content.text:
The one finding was the mismatch between the Brief Description of FIG. 6 and the FIG. 6 brief over what is cut at the break. Fixed by adopting the first of the two alternatives, which keeps the hatching that makes the segment ends read as solid bodies.

**`draft/07-drawings.md`** now reads that FIG. 6 is viewed with the near frame wall broken away "and the frame and the cam ring segments shown in section at the break," matching the two-slant hatching in the brief.

**`figures/FIG-6.md`** opening sentence was aligned to the same statement: the frame and the two cam ring segments are shown in section at the break so that the segment ends are seen. The rest of the brief is unchanged, so the segment ends still carry hatching at a slant different from the frame hatching, and the leaders for 22 and 24 still land on that hatching.

Nothing else moved: the detailed description's account of FIG. 6 makes no statement about what is cut, and the claims, numeral table and FIG. 4 were untouched. FIG. 6's brief is 2717 characters and FIG. 4's is 2698, both inside the limit, with the other four at 2363, 2313, 2183 and 1674.

input.summary: Fixed the single reported inconsistency, the disagreement between the Brief Description of FIG. 6 and the FIG. 6 brief about which parts are cut at the break. draft/07-drawings.md now states that the frame and the cam ring segments are shown in section at the break, matching the two slant hatching already specified in figures/FIG-6.md, and the opening sentence of figures/FIG-6.md was aligned to the same statement so that both documents say the frame and the two cam ring segments are shown in section at the break and the segment ends are seen. The rest of the FIG. 6 brief is unchanged: the segment ends keep section hatching at a slant different from the frame hatching, which is what makes them read as solid bodies rather than as voids in the guide channels, and the leaders for 22 and 24 still land on that hatching. The detailed description says nothing about what is cut at the break, so no change was needed there, and the claims, numeral table and FIG. 4 were untouched. FIG. 6's brief measures 2717 characters and FIG. 4's 2698, with the remaining four at 2363, 2313, 2183 and 1674, all inside the limit.
reasoning: The finding offered two mutually exclusive cures, and I took the one that keeps the hatching. Returning the segment ends to plain outline would undo the fix that stopped them rendering as empty space inside the hatched channels, so the cheaper correction was to bring the Brief Description into line with the brief rather than the other way round.

I changed the brief's own first sentence as well, because it still said the break made the segment ends visible while a later sentence hatched them. Saying in both places that the frame and the segments are shown in section at the break leaves no room for a reader to wonder whether those ends are cut surfaces or exposed faces.

Nothing about the invention moved. What is cut at a break is a depiction convention, not structure, and the detailed description's account of the latch end joint is silent on it, so the claims, the numeral table, the detailed description and FIG. 4 all stay as filed and remain in step with the briefs.
The added words cost characters, so I checked the length gate again before returning: FIG. 6 sits at 2717 and FIG. 4 at 2698, both under the 2800 limit, and no sheet lists more than eight numerals.

content:
The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

1	Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.
2	
3	A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe, in the manner of a band or a two-bolt saddle, transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. Such an arrangement is commonly supplied with liners or inserts machined for one nominal pipe size, and a different pipe size calls for a different insert or a different clamp.
4	
5	Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Thin walled tube, coated pipe, and lined pipe are all damaged by that kind of concentrated loading, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. Torque tools and gauges can be added to the installation, but they add a separate instrument to the task and, when they respond to the position of the gripping elements, they report the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.
6	
7	What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.
8

Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.

A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe, in the manner of a band or a two-bolt saddle, transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. Such an arrangement is commonly supplied with liners or inserts machined for one nominal pipe size, and a different pipe size calls for a different insert or a different clamp.

Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Thin walled tube, coated pipe, and lined pipe are all damaged by that kind of concentrated loading, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. Torque tools and gauges can be added to the installation, but they add a separate instrument to the task and, when they respond to the position of the gripping elements, they report the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.

A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. An arrangement of that kind depends on a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, so that a different pipe size calls for a different part.

Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Thin walled tube, coated pipe, and lined pipe are all damaged by that kind of concentrated loading, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. Torque tools and gauges can be added to the installation, but they add a separate instrument to the task and, when they respond to the position of the gripping elements, they report the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.

What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the frame axis from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown, the frame and the two cam ring segments being shown in section at the break so that the segment ends are seen. Here the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and radially outward is toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and the two segment ends. Cut frame material carries section hatching, and each segment end carries section hatching of its own at a slant different from that of the frame hatching. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the extent of the break at the radially outer side of each body.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one the lower part, with a parting line between them running the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12. Each body is bounded on the left by an upright edge, on the right by an irregular break line, and toward the parting line by a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right.

The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left edge of its body, so a band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and that edge. In the upper body a further band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and the break line at its right. In the lower body the frame wall radially outside the channel is interrupted, as in FIG. 4, so the radially outer side of the block in that channel is exposed, the break line at the right of that body lying beyond that exposed side.

A solid block filled with its own hatching lies in each channel and reaches along it to the end face of its body without passing beyond it. The block in the upper body is the first cam ring segment 22 and the block in the lower body is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line.

At the parting line the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 lie against one another in contact across the full width of the blocks, filling the parting line where they meet. Those surfaces in contact are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the upper body, away from the parting line.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the lower body, away from the parting line.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the horizontal contact between the end faces of the two blocks at the parting line.

Two of the three findings were file-level and are fixed; the third is a rendering gap.

**Background (`draft/05-background.md`).** The unsourced prior-art specifics are gone. The pull-closed sentence no longer names particular constructions and now ends with the supported point: an arrangement of that kind depends on a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, so a different pipe size calls for a different part. The damage sentence and the named instruments are replaced by what the disclosure supports: concentrated loading of a single gripping surface is undesirable and the operator has no indication that it has occurred, and an added instrument that responds to the position of the gripping elements reports the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip. Those track the disclosure's own "without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter" and "reports clamp loading mechanically and does not measure pipe diameter." The uneven-loading mechanism, which the disclosure does support, is untouched, and no other section carried the removed assertions.

**FIG. 6 leader for numeral 18.** It now targets the surface of the channel wall in the upper body on the radially outer side of the block lying in the channel, the same convention FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 already use, so 18 no longer lands in the same body of first-frame-half material as 10. reasoning: The Background rewrite kept the technical problem and dropped only what had no source. The disclosure supports a clamp that grips without a tool-specific pipe diameter and an indicator that reports loading rather than diameter, so the diameter-dependent part and the instrument that reports size rather than force both survive in functional terms. What went was the list of particular prior constructions and the assertion that particular pipe types are damaged, which is a factual result about existing equipment that neither the disclosure nor any reference in the workspace supports.

I left the paragraph about separately driven gripping surfaces alone. The disclosure itself describes forcing one jaw farther than the others, so the uneven-loading mechanism is supported, and it is the problem the coupled ring and the force-limiting spring stack exist to solve. Removing it would have stripped the specification of the explanation a later argument is built from.

For numeral 18 in FIG. 6 the defect was that both bands of hatched material flanking the upper channel are the same physical body, the first frame half, so a leader into either band labels the part that 10 already labels. Pointing 18 at the channel wall surface makes it label the guide, and it matches how FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 already target the same part, which keeps the three sheets consistent with one another.

I did not touch FIG. 3 or FIG. 5 despite their semantic pixel entries. The reviewer established that neither has a stored image, so there is no verified visual defect to correct, and editing a brief on the strength of a check that never saw pixels would risk degrading a brief that is currently complete and consistent.

No image files were created for the empty drawing set. Figure specifications are Markdown by rule and the sheets are produced by the pipeline from the briefs, so the correct response to the numeral-coverage failure was to leave every numeral definition and brief intact for rendering rather than to prune the specification to match an empty figures directory.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity, the interruption in the frame wall, the length of the ring drive face 36, the attitude and mounting of the latch handle 50, its action on the force-limiting spring stack 54, that stack drawn as one spring symbol, and the direction in which the wedge 52 advances with the resulting movement of the bands.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second hatched body holds a like band from the right. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing the upper side of that band. Near the right end of that exposed side the ring drive face 36 is one straight surface, its left end high at the level of the exposed upper side and its right end low within the band, so the face descends from left to right, toward the parting line. Its right end stops short of that line, a short piece of the exposed upper side running on from it to the line.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward over the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity; its lower face descends from left to right at the same slant and rests on the ring drive face 36 along its length, so downward movement of the wedge 52 presses the left band toward the left.

Above the wedge 52 the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 to the latch handle 50 beside its pivot, so the stack lies between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity and runs up and to the right through an opening where the top and right walls stop short of one another, leaning past upright, the over-center position; it is a straight bar of even width.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall and projects beyond the outer surface of that wall, the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 against which its position is read.

- 50 latch handle: target well inside the straight bar.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.

A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. An arrangement of that kind depends on a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, so that a different pipe size calls for a different part.

Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Concentrated loading of a single gripping surface is undesirable, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. An added instrument that responds to the position of the gripping elements reports the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.

What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.

If the gripping surfaces of each part are driven separately, the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive is given up: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. If the split body is instead pulled closed on the pipe, the closing force passes through the joint at the split and the pipe itself reacts the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe, and a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is needed, so that a different pipe size calls for a different part.

Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Concentrated loading of a single gripping surface is undesirable, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. An added instrument that responds to the position of the gripping elements reports the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.

What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.

To keep FIG. 4 inside the length limit I removed only redundancy: a repeated naming of the handle and wedge around the spring stack, a schematic clause duplicating the wedge direction that the body already states positively, and a wordy description of the housing opening.

**Background (`draft/05-background.md`).** The two sentences are now conditional statements of the engineering problem rather than assertions about existing arrangements: if the gripping surfaces of each part are driven separately, the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive is given up, with the consequences that follow; if the split body is instead pulled closed on the pipe, the closing force passes through the joint at the split and the pipe reacts the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore matches the pipe and a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is needed. # FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching, the wedge 52, the latch housing 58 and each cam ring segment each at a slant different from that of the frame bodies that hold them; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity, the interruption in the frame wall, the length of the ring drive face 36, the attitude and mounting of the latch handle 50, its action on the force-limiting spring stack 54, that stack drawn as one spring symbol, and the direction in which the wedge 52 advances.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second hatched body holds a like band from the right. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing the upper side of that band. Near the right end of that exposed side the ring drive face 36 is one straight surface, its left end high at the level of the exposed upper side and its right end low within the band, so the face descends from left to right, toward the parting line. Its right end stops short of that line, a short piece of the exposed upper side running on from it to the line.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward over the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity; its lower face descends from left to right at the same slant and rests on the ring drive face 36 along its length, so downward movement of the wedge 52 presses the left band toward the left.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 to the latch handle 50 beside its pivot, so the stack lies between them.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity and runs up and to the right through an opening between the top and right walls, leaning past upright, the over-center position; it is a straight bar of even width.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall and projects beyond the outer surface of that wall, the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 against which its position is read.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching of the right band.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the straight bar.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the positions and tilt of the three slots, and the position and length of the ring drive face 36.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between the two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26. At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer. The three are alike and all tilt the same way: in each, the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary.

The ring drive face 36 is a short straight flat cut into the outer boundary of the second cam ring segment 24, in the arc running downward from the right joint. Its upper end, the end nearer that joint, lies radially inside the outer boundary and stops below the joint, so a short piece of the circular outer boundary runs on from it to the joint. Its lower end, further from the joint, meets the circular outer boundary. Between the two ends the flat is one straight edge, so the material cut from the segment is deepest at the upper end and runs out to nothing at the lower end. Elsewhere both outer boundaries are circular.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the outer boundary in the upper right.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper segment.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower segment.
- 26 complementary coupling faces at the hinge end: target the surfaces meeting at the left joint.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the right joint.
- 34 oblique slot: target well inside the opening near the top.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface near the right joint.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body carry hatching at a slant different from that of every other cut element it touches or lies beside in the view; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity, the interruption in the frame wall, the length of the ring drive face 36, the attitude and mounting of the latch handle 50, its action on the force-limiting spring stack 54, that stack drawn as one spring symbol, and the direction in which the wedge 52 advances.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second hatched body holds a like band from the right. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing the upper side of that band. Near the right end of that exposed side the ring drive face 36 is one straight surface, its left end high at the level of the exposed upper side and its right end low within the band, so the face descends from left to right, toward the parting line. Its right end stops short of that line, a short piece of the exposed upper side running on from it to the line.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward over the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity; its lower face descends from left to right at the same slant and rests on the ring drive face 36 along its length, so downward movement of the wedge 52 presses the left band toward the left.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 to the latch handle 50 beside its pivot, so the stack lies between them.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity and runs up and to the right through an opening between the top and right walls, leaning past upright, the over-center position; it is a straight bar of even width.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall and projects beyond the outer surface of that wall, the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 against which its position is read.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the frame axis from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown, the frame and the two cam ring segments being shown in section at the break so that the segment ends are seen. Here the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and radially outward is toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and the two segment ends. Cut material carries section hatching; the upper frame body, the lower frame body and each of the two cam ring segments carry hatching at a slant different from that of every other cut element it touches, so the parting line and the contact between the segment end faces stay distinct. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the extent of the break at the radially outer side of each body.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, filling the upper and lower parts of the view, with a parting line between them running the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12. Each body is bounded on the left by an upright edge, on the right by an irregular break line, and toward the parting line by a straight horizontal end face.

The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left edge of its body, so a band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and that edge. In the upper body a further band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and the break line at its right. In the lower body the frame wall radially outside the channel is interrupted, as in FIG. 4, so the radially outer side of the block in that channel is exposed, the break line at the right of that body lying beyond that exposed side.

A solid block lies in each channel and reaches along it to the end face of its body without passing beyond it. The block in the upper body is the first cam ring segment 22 and the block in the lower body is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line.

At the parting line the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 lie against one another in contact across the full width of the blocks, filling the parting line where they meet. Those surfaces in contact are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Both findings are fixed.

**Hatching of juxtaposed elements.** `figures/FIG-4.md` now requires that the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body carry hatching at a slant different from every other cut element it touches or lies beside in the view. `figures/FIG-6.md` requires the same of the upper frame body, the lower frame body and each of the two cam ring segments, and states the reason: the parting line and the contact between the segment end faces must stay distinct, which is exactly what that sheet exists to show. FIG. 3 already distinguishes the cam ring and the jaw carriage from the frame body, and no two different elements touch there without that distinction.

**FIG. 2 and the coupled condition.** All three places now use the isolated-subassembly wording. `draft/07-drawings.md`: shown removed from the frame, the cam ring segments being drawn in the relative positions they occupy when coupled in the closed condition. `draft/08-detailed-description.md`: the same, for the segmented cam ring 20. `figures/FIG-2.md`: its two segments drawn in the relative positions they occupy when coupled in the closed condition. Nothing now asserts a coupled state for a ring outside the frame, so the sheet no longer contradicts the description's account that closing the frame halves makes the coupling and opening them breaks it.

The added text needed room, so I trimmed duplication in the same two briefs: in FIG. 4 a schematic disclaimer for the wedge direction that the body already states positively, plus two wordy phrases; in FIG. 6 a purpose clause the Brief Description carries and a redundant mention of the blocks' hatching, now covered by the view statement. Brief bodies stand at 2363, 2386, 2304, 2723, 1674 and 2722 characters, all inside the limit, and the claims, numeral table and the rest of the description are unchanged.

input.summary: Both findings fixed. figures/FIG-4.md now requires the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body to carry hatching at a slant different from every other cut element it touches or lies beside in the view, and figures/FIG-6.md requires the same of the upper frame body, the lower frame body and each of the two cam ring segments, stating that the parting line and the contact between the segment end faces must stay distinct. The FIG. 2 coupled-condition wording was corrected in all three places: draft/07-drawings.md and draft/08-detailed-description.md now say the segments are drawn in the relative positions they occupy when coupled in the closed condition, and figures/FIG-2.md says the same, so nothing asserts a coupled state for a ring lying outside the frame. To keep both briefs within the length limit I removed only duplication: in FIG. 4 a schematic disclaimer for the wedge direction that the body already states positively plus two wordy phrases, and in FIG. 6 a purpose clause the Brief Description already carries and a redundant mention of the blocks' hatching now covered by the view statement. Brief bodies stand at 2363, 2386, 2304, 2723, 1674 and 2722 characters, and the claims, numeral table and the remainder of the description are unchanged and in step.
reasoning: The hatching rule was stated only against the frame, which left the pairs that matter unprotected: the wedge sits inside and bears on the latch housing, the two frame bodies meet at the parting line, and in FIG. 6 the two segment ends touch at the very interface the sheet exists to show. Stating the requirement pairwise, against every cut element a body touches or lies beside, covers those pairs without naming a slant for any of them, which keeps the brief free of invented rendering values.

In FIG. 6 I kept the reason in the sentence, that the parting line and the segment contact stay distinct, because the requirement and its purpose travel together: a renderer that knows why the slants must differ is less likely to merge the two blocks into one body, which was the earlier failure mode on that sheet.

The FIG. 2 wording was a genuine internal contradiction rather than a drawing artifact. The description defines the coupled condition as made by closing the frame halves and broken by opening them, so a ring drawn outside the frame cannot be in it. The isolated-subassembly phrasing keeps the figure showing exactly the same geometry, the segment ends meeting at the coupling faces, without asserting a state the specification says cannot exist there.

Both edits added characters to briefs that had little headroom, so I paid for them out of duplication rather than geometry. The wedge direction clause in the FIG. 4 schematic list was worse than redundant, since the downward advance and the resulting leftward push are required relationships stated positively in the body, and flagging that direction as schematic worked against the text.

Nothing in the claims or the numeral table moved, and the only description change is the FIG. 2 sentence, which the finding identified. Which parts are cut and how they are hatched is a depiction convention, so it belongs in the briefs, and the Brief Description entry for FIG. 6 already says the frame and the cam ring segments are shown in section at the break, which is consistent with the new hatching sentence.

sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add

sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's right being the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis runs left to right. A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left, the two meeting.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. One short rectangular opening passes through that block from its left face to its right face; apart from that opening the block is solid and hatched throughout. The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

Nothing in the patent text moved this turn. content:
The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.

false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the split pipe clamp closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

The pipe 90 is seen end on at the centre of the drawing area and appears as one circle, the area within it blank. An annular frame body surrounds it, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from the pipe 90 and by an outer circle. The ring-shaped space between the pipe 90 and that inner circle is open, crossed only by the jaw pads 40 and the inner ends of the jaw carriages 30.

Two radial joint lines, at the left and at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10, the lower the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, shown schematically as a small circle on that joint line between the inner circle and the outer circle, with a short block reaching to it from each frame end, the whole hinge 14 lying within the width of the frame body.

At the right joint is the latch 16, shown schematically as a rectangular block outside the frame body bridging both frame ends, with a lever reaching radially outward from it, inclined toward the first frame half 10, the over-center attitude.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the annular frame body, at the top, the lower left and the lower right, the topmost on the first frame half 10 and the others on the second frame half 12. At each position the inner circle is interrupted by a radial opening and the jaw carriage 30 is shown schematically as a block reaching radially inward through that opening, its outer portion within the body and its inner end inside the inner circle.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined at a small circle, a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the pipe 90.

A short broken cutting-plane line lies in the upper part of the view on the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30, its outer end just outside the outer circle and its inner end at the pipe 90. A short arrow at each end points horizontally to the right, both on the same side of the line, giving the direction in which FIG. 3 is viewed. Each end carries the numeral 3 as the section designation, just outside that end beside its arrow, so the line reads as line 3-3; it is not a reference numeral.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer circle of the frame body at the upper left, away from the pipe 90.
- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper semicircular body.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower semicircular body.
- 14 hinge: target the small circle at the left joint.
- 16 latch: target the rectangular block bridging the right joint.
- 30 jaw carriage: target well inside the topmost carriage block.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the member at the topmost carriage inner end.
- 90 pipe: target the interior of the central circle, inside the inner circle.

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body carry hatching at a slant different from that of every other cut element it touches or lies beside in the view; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity, the interruption in the frame wall, the length of the ring drive face 36, the attitude and mounting of the latch handle 50, its action on the force-limiting spring stack 54, and that stack drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band from the right. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing the upper side of that band. Near the right end of that exposed side the ring drive face 36 is one straight surface, its left end high at the level of the exposed upper side and its right end low within the band, so the face descends from left to right, toward the parting line. Its right end stops short of that line, a short piece of the exposed upper side running on from it to the line.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward over the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity; its lower face descends from left to right at the same slant and rests on the ring drive face 36 along its length, so downward movement of the wedge 52 presses the left band toward the left.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 to the latch handle 50 beside its pivot, so the stack lies between them.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity and runs up and to the right through an opening between the top and right walls, leaning past upright, the over-center position; it is a straight bar of even width.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall and projects beyond the outer surface of that wall, the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 against which its position is read.

The blocking cause is unchanged and I verified it directly: a workspace-wide search for `*.png`, `*.svg` and `*.json` returns nothing, so no sheet has been rendered and `review/figure-audit-evidence.json` does not exist. All four mechanical entries trace to that one absence, and the finding states that no specification text, claim, numeral definition or brief wording needs to change to cure it.

I made two small refinements to the briefs, both required by the standing drafting rules rather than by the finding, and neither touching the invention:

- **`figures/FIG-1.md`** no longer prescribes that the pipe 90 "appears as one circle." That was a face-linework control of the kind the instructions say to remove. It now reads as positive geometry: the pipe 90 is seen end on at the centre of the drawing area as a circle with its interior blank. The separation that matters is still carried positively by the next sentence, where the ring-shaped space between the pipe and the frame's inner circle is open and crossed only by the jaw pads 40 and the inner ends of the jaw carriages 30.
- **`figures/FIG-4.md`** now declares the outline of the latch handle 50 as schematic alongside its attitude and mounting, so the straight bar of even width is properly identified as a depiction convention rather than an asserted shape. The claims and description remain shape-neutral about the handle.

Everything else is untouched and verified in step: each brief's body numerals match its own list, no sheet lists more than eight numerals, the six lists place all 26 numerals of `draft/numerals.md` with none unplaced and none on two parts, the 3-3 designation is identical in FIG. 1, FIG. 3, the Brief Description and the detailed description, and the brief bodies measure 2347, 2386, 2404, 2732, 1883 and 2722 characters.

What closes this gate is rendering `figures/rendered-FIG-1.png` through `rendered-FIG-6.png` from these briefs and regenerating the audit evidence against the resulting image hashes. Figure files here are Markdown specifications and the pixels come from the image pipeline, so I did not create image or evidence files.

All four mechanical entries trace to that single absence, and the finding states that no specification text, claim, numeral definition or brief wording needs to change to cure it, so I left the certified text and the numeral allocations alone. I made two small brief refinements required by the standing drafting rules rather than by the finding, neither touching the invention: figures/FIG-1.md no longer prescribes that the pipe 90 appears as one circle, which was a face-linework control, and now states positively that the pipe 90 is seen end on at the centre of the drawing area as a circle with its interior blank, the separation from the frame's inner circle still being carried by the open ring-shaped space crossed only by the jaw pads 40 and the inner ends of the jaw carriages 30; and figures/FIG-4.md now declares the outline of the latch handle 50 schematic alongside its attitude and mounting, so the straight bar of even width reads as a depiction convention rather than an asserted shape. Everything else is verified in step: each brief's body numerals match its own list, no sheet lists more than eight numerals, the six lists place all 26 numerals with none unplaced and none on two parts, the 3-3 designation is identical in FIG. 1, FIG. 3, the Brief Description and the detailed description, and the brief bodies measure 2347, 2386, 2404, 2732, 1883 and 2722 characters. Rendering the six sheets from these briefs and regenerating the audit evidence is what closes the gate.
reasoning: I checked the cause myself rather than taking the report at face value: a recursive search for image and json files across the workspace returns nothing at all. That rules out a render that produced bad pixels and points to sheets never landing here, which is consistent with the numeral check reporting every numeral missing and with FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 being described as having stored sheets that are not on disk.

I did not fabricate image or evidence files. Figure specifications in this workspace are Markdown, the pipeline draws the geometry and places numerals, leaders and section annotation deterministically from them, and the audit evidence is bound to the resulting image hashes. A file written by hand would assert a verification that never happened.

The two edits I did make come from the standing instructions, not from the finding. Prescribing that the pipe appears as one circle is exactly the kind of one-stroke outline control the rules say to replace with positive geometry, and it is no longer needed: the open ring-shaped band between the pipe and the frame's inner circle, crossed only by the pads and carriage ends, is what keeps those two circles apart.

Declaring the latch handle outline schematic closes a smaller gap of the same kind. The disclosure gives a latch handle but no shape, so the straight bar of even width is a depiction convention; naming it as one in the brief keeps an undisclosed shape from reading as an embodiment while leaving the claims and description shape-neutral.

I deliberately left everything the review certified untouched, including the pairwise hatching rule now stated on all four sectioned sheets, the isolated-subassembly wording for FIG. 2 and every numeral target. Two turns of this gate have failed on the same physical cause, and editing certified text to look responsive would risk introducing a defect where none exists.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring removed from the frame, its two segments drawn in the relative positions they occupy when coupled in the closed condition, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the positions and tilt of the three slots, and the position and length of the ring drive face 36.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between the two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26. At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer. The three are alike and all tilt the same way: in each, the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary.

The ring drive face 36 is a short straight flat cut into the outer boundary of the second cam ring segment 24, in the arc running downward from the right joint. Its upper end, the end nearer that joint, lies radially inside the outer boundary and stops below the joint, so a short piece of the circular outer boundary runs on from it to the joint. Its lower end, further from the joint, meets the circular outer boundary. Between the two ends the flat is one straight edge, so the material cut from the segment is deepest at the upper end and runs out to nothing at the lower end. Elsewhere both outer boundaries are circular.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body carry hatching at a slant different from that of every other cut element it touches or lies beside in the view; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity, the interruption in the frame wall, the length of the ring drive face 36, the attitude, outline and mounting of the latch handle 50, its action on the force-limiting spring stack 54, and that stack drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band from the right. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing the upper side of that band. Near the right end of that exposed side the ring drive face 36 is one straight surface, its left end high at the level of the exposed upper side and its right end low within the band, so the face descends from left to right, toward the parting line. Its right end stops short of that line, a short piece of the exposed upper side running on from it to the line.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward over the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity; its lower face descends from left to right at the same slant and rests on the ring drive face 36 along its length, so downward movement of the wedge 52 presses the left band toward the left.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 to the latch handle 50 beside its pivot, so the stack lies between them.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity and runs up and to the right through an opening between the top and right walls, leaning past upright, the over-center position; it is a straight bar of even width.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall and projects beyond the outer surface of that wall, the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 against which its position is read.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching of the right band.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the straight bar.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

content.text:
Both findings are fixed inside the figure briefs, with no change to the specification.

**Ring drive face form and depth.** `figures/FIG-2.md` now declares as schematic "the position, length, form and depth of the ring drive face 36," so the flat cut into the outer boundary and its depth gradient read as depiction choices rather than asserted structure. `figures/FIG-4.md` correspondingly declares "the length, form and slant of the ring drive face 36." The description remains as it was, saying only that the face lies at an inclination to the direction in which the wedge 52 advances.

**Wedge advance direction and lower-face slant.** `figures/FIG-4.md` now also declares as schematic "the direction in which the wedge 52 advances and the slant of its lower face." The two sheets still show a consistent, renderable drive geometry, but nothing in them stands as an assertion about a direction the disclosure does not give. The description continues to say only that the wedge has an inclined face bearing on the ring drive face 36 and that latch movement advances it against that face.

The added declarations needed room in FIG. 4, so I removed only redundancy there: a trailing restatement that the spring stack lies between the handle and the wedge, which the same sentence already conveys by running it from the wedge up to the handle, and four short wordings condensed without losing a body, contact or direction. FIG. 4's brief is 2743 characters and FIG. 2's is 2399, both within the limit, and the claims, description, numeral table and drawing descriptions are untouched and in step.

input.summary: Both minor findings are fixed by extending the schematic declarations inside the figure briefs, with no change to the specification. figures/FIG-2.md now declares as schematic the position, length, form and depth of the ring drive face 36, so the flat cut into the ring's outer boundary and its depth gradient read as depiction choices rather than asserted structure, and figures/FIG-4.md declares the length, form and slant of the same face. figures/FIG-4.md also declares as schematic the direction in which the wedge 52 advances and the slant of its lower face, so no direction of wedge travel stands as an invention assertion. The detailed description is unchanged and still says only that the ring drive face lies at an inclination to the direction in which the wedge advances and that the wedge has an inclined face advanced against that face. The added declarations needed room in FIG. 4, so I removed only redundancy there: a trailing restatement that the spring stack lies between the handle and the wedge, which the same sentence conveys by running the stack from the wedge up to the handle, plus four short condensations that drop no body, contact or direction. FIG. 4's brief is 2743 characters and FIG. 2's is 2399, both within the limit, and the claims, description, numeral table and drawing descriptions are untouched and synchronized.
reasoning: Both findings are about the same failure mode: a render-time geometric choice that carries technical substance because it fixes the rotation sense of the coupled ring, sitting outside the schematic declaration that would mark it as a depiction convention. The cure is to widen the declaration, not to change the geometry, because the sheets still need one internally consistent drive geometry to render at all.

I kept the drive geometry exactly as it stands. FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 agree on which segment carries the face, which end is deepest and which way the wedge presses, and that agreement is what earlier reviews verified. Removing the slant would have left the renderer free to draw a face that no longer converts wedge travel into the ring rotation the oblique slots need.

Nothing was added to the specification. The description already speaks only of an inclination to the direction of wedge advance and an inclined wedge face, which is the level of detail the disclosure supports, so the claims and description stay neutral while the briefs carry the depiction choices under an explicit schematic flag.

FIG. 4 had about twenty characters of headroom once both declarations went in, so I paid for them out of duplication. The clearest case was the clause saying the spring stack lies between the handle and the wedge: the same sentence already describes it rising from the wedge to the handle, and the disclosed relationship is stated in full in the detailed description and recited in claim 1.

I left the numeral targets, the hatching rule and every structural sentence alone. The review certified the source ledger, the numeral assignments and the cross-figure geometry, so the only edits this turn are the two declarations the findings named and the trimming needed to fit them.

content:
The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,

The final step now reads continuing to move the latch handle into the second, over-center position after all three jaw pads have seated on the pipe, which is definite and no longer presupposes an act that was never recited. Antecedents run clean through the chain: the latch comes from the opening step, a latch handle of the latch and a wedge are introduced in the fifth step and picked up definitely in the final step, and a second, over-center position is introduced in the fifth step and referred to definitely afterward. Claims 14 and 15 needed no change, since the force-limiting spring stack is introduced in the final step of claim 13 and releasing the latch refers to the latch of the first step. Scope is unchanged, the description already recites the same act at draft/08, and no figure brief, numeral or other claim required a change.
reasoning: The defect was that one step said continuing while introducing the handle indefinitely, so the claim both presupposed a prior movement of the handle and announced the handle as new. Moving the introduction back to the fifth step, which is the step that actually starts the handle moving, cures both halves at once and leaves the sequence of acts exactly as it was.

I took the handle into the fifth step rather than deleting continuing from the last step, because the continuation is the point of that limitation: the residual travel after the pads seat is what the force limiting spring stack absorbs, and that is the relationship the disclosure gives and claim 1 recites on the apparatus side.

Scope did not move. Moving the latch and moving its handle are the same act in this clamp, the description already says the operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second over-center position, and the disclosure describes both the latch reaching the over-center position and additional handle travel after the pads contact the pipe.

I checked the rest of the chain rather than assuming: the wedge and the over-center position are introduced in the amended fifth step and taken up definitely in the final one, the spring stack is introduced in the final step which claim 14 then refers to, and claim 15 releases the latch introduced in the first step. Nothing else needed touching.

I left the Summary's method paragraph as it stands, saying the operator moves the latch to the over-center position. That tracks the disclosure's own wording, is not claim language, and creates no inconsistency with a claim that recites the handle as the part moved.

draft/09-claims.md, claim 13 final step: now recites continuing to move the latch handle into the second, over-center position, making the reference definite
data.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the draft contains no citation, so there is no reference to distinguish or mischaracterise. The Background states the problem conditionally, and each problem it states is answered by a feature recited in claim 1 and tracked by method claim 13: cam ring segments recoupled by the act of closing the frame so that one latch input reaches all three jaw carriages through a single coupled ring, follower and oblique slot pairs that convert that rotation into synchronized radial travel, and a force limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge that absorbs the operator's remaining handle travel instead of driving one jaw harder than the others. This turn changed only the antecedent wording of two steps and no limitation's scope.
